passages.t: The widow and the unjust judge
passages.happening:
Jesus tells his disciples a parable “about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart” (verse 1).

In a certain town there was a judge “who neither feared God nor respected men” (verse 2). A widow in that town kept coming to him: ‘Give me justice against my adversary’ (verse 3). For a while he refused. But at last he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect men, yet because this widow keeps pestering me, I will give her justice. Then she will stop wearing me out with her perpetual requests’ (verses 4-5).

“Listen to the words of the unjust judge,” says the Lord. “Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night? Will He continue to defer their help? I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?” (verses 6-8).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this parable.

A widow in Jesus' world was often left without a husband to speak for her in public or to protect her property. Again and again the Law named widows, with orphans and foreigners, as people God himself would defend. A judge was meant to do the same. This one cares for neither God nor anyone else. He cannot be shamed and he does not care what is right.

The widow has only one weapon: she will not stop coming. And the judge, who is afraid of nothing, becomes afraid of her. The word Luke uses for ‘wearing me out’ is a boxer's word. It means to hit someone under the eye, to give them a black eye. The only other place it appears in the New Testament is where Paul speaks of disciplining his body like a boxer (1 Corinthians 9:27). The powerful judge, in his own words, is worried that this widow will beat him up. Jesus' hearers would have smiled.

Then Jesus draws the lesson, and he draws it by contrast. If even a corrupt judge will finally act for someone he does not care about, how much more will God act for those he has chosen and loves. A Jewish wisdom book called Sirach, written before Jesus' time, had already said that the Lord does not ignore the widow when she pours out her complaint, and many readers hear that teaching behind this parable.

The story comes right after Jesus' words about the days of the Son of Man (17:22-37). His followers will face a long wait, with injustice all around them. The danger is that they will stop praying, and stop believing that God will ever act. So the parable ends with a question to them: when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith?
passages.ot:
The Law spoke for God: “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:22-23). God is called “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows” (Psalm 68:5). And the prophets condemned rulers who would not hear a widow: “They do not defend the fatherless, and the plea of the widow never comes before them” (Isaiah 1:23).

The Psalms know what long waiting feels like: “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1).
passages.hard:
Is God like the unjust judge, someone who has to be nagged into acting? No. The parable works by contrast, not by likeness. The judge does not fear God; God is God. The judge does not care about the widow; God calls his people “His elect” and hears them “day and night”. The judge acts only to be left alone; God acts because he is just and he loves. Prayer is not wearing God down until he gives in. It is refusing to give up on a God who is good, even when his answer seems slow.

But what about ‘He will promptly carry out justice’, when so many have waited so long? This is a real difficulty, and the Bible does not hide it. Its own prayers ask “How long?”, and in the book of Revelation even the martyrs cry out, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10). Many readers take ‘promptly’ to mean that when God's justice comes, it will come suddenly and without further delay, not that it will always come soon by our clocks. The parable does not explain the waiting. It tells us how to wait: praying, and not losing heart.

A word to anyone who has prayed for years for justice and seen none, or who has been failed by a court, by the police, or by a church that should have listened. Jesus does not say that the failure was right. The judge in this story is called unjust, and Jesus calls him that himself. God is not like him. Your cries are not wearing God out; he hears them. Keep telling the truth to people who can help: a lawyer, an advocate, the proper authorities, a pastor you trust. If you are in danger, contact the police or a crisis line. And if a church failed you, that failure was theirs, not God's.
passages.asks: The widow kept coming back. Ask what you have stopped praying for because the answer seemed too slow. Bring it again. And ask whom you know who is crying out for justice right now. Sometimes God answers a widow's prayer through people who will stand with her.

passages.t: The Pharisee and the tax collector
passages.happening:
Jesus tells this parable to some “who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt” (verse 9).

“Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (verse 10). The Pharisee stands by himself and prays, ‘God, I thank You that I am not like the other men’, cheats, wrongdoers, adulterers, ‘or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire’ (verses 11-12).

“But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’” (verse 13).

“I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this parable.

The Pharisees were a movement of devout Jews who tried to keep God's law in the whole of ordinary life, at home and at work, not only in the temple (see the note on 11:37-44). Many ordinary people admired them. So ‘Pharisee’ is not a word for a hypocrite. In later Christian speech it came to mean that, but it did not mean that to Jesus' hearers. To them, the Pharisee in this story was the good man, the one you would want your son to grow up like. Everything he says about his life may be true.

He does more than the Law asked. The Law commanded one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). He fasts twice a week. A very early Christian handbook called the Didache says that some fasted on Mondays and Thursdays, and told Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays instead, so twice-weekly fasting was a known practice. The Law asked for a tenth of the harvest (Deuteronomy 14:22). He gives a tenth of everything he gets.

Tax collectors were local men who collected taxes and tolls for the rulers, Rome or Herod's family, and many made money by charging more than was owed (see the note on 3:12-14). They were widely despised as cheats who worked for foreign rulers.

People usually prayed standing and looking up (as Jesus does in John 17:1). The tax collector stands far back, will not lift his eyes, and beats his breast, a sign of deep grief. Luke uses the same picture at the cross, where the crowds go home ‘beating their breasts’ (23:48). His prayer is seven words in the BSB. It has no list of good deeds and no comparison with anyone. It is only the truth and a cry for mercy. The Greek word for ‘have mercy’ here is not the one Luke uses for the blind man's cry (verse 38). It is the same verb that Hebrews uses for Jesus making atonement for the sins of the people (Hebrews 2:17). Some readers hear in it a man asking God to accept him on the ground of the sacrifice, not of his own life.

Then the shock. The tax collector, not the Pharisee, ‘went home justified’, which means declared right with God. Jesus' hearers would have gasped.

His prayer has been prayed by Christians ever since. The Eastern churches' Jesus Prayer, ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me’, grew in part from cries like his and the blind man's.
passages.ot:
The tax collector prays like the psalmist: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions” (Psalm 51:1). And the same psalm says what God wants: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

God says through Isaiah, “I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the contrite” (Isaiah 57:15).
passages.hard:
Is this parable a verdict on Pharisees, or on Jews? No. Over the centuries Christians have used it to sneer at Jews and Judaism as proud and empty. That reading is wrong, and it turns the parable upside down. Both men in the story are Jews, praying in the Jewish temple, to the God of Israel. The tax collector's prayer comes straight from Israel's own Psalms. And Luke shows Pharisees inviting Jesus to their tables (7:36; 11:37; 14:1) and warning him of danger (13:31). Verse 9 does not say ‘Pharisees’. It names a kind of person: anyone who trusts in their own goodness and looks down on others.

That is the point, and it is a trap for every reader. The quickest way to become the Pharisee in this story is to pray, ‘God, I thank you that I am not like that Pharisee.’ The ‘Pharisee’ Jesus warns against is not in first-century Jerusalem. He is in the listener: in the church member who is quietly glad not to be like those people, in the reader who already knows which character they are. The parable is told to religious people, and it speaks first to the church.

Does Jesus condemn fasting and giving? No. He fasted and taught about giving himself. The Pharisee's fault is not his practices. It is that he trusts them, and that he holds others in contempt. He goes to the temple to pray, and ends up talking about himself.
passages.asks: Read the Pharisee's prayer again and ask whether any of it sounds like you, even in a quieter form. Then try the tax collector's prayer, slowly and honestly: ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner.’ It is a prayer for anyone, on any day, and God hears it.

passages.happening:
People are bringing even their babies to Jesus, so that he will place his hands on them. When the disciples see this, they rebuke those who brought them.

But Jesus calls the children to him and says, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this scene too (Mark 10:13-16; Matthew 19:13-15). Children in the ancient world were loved by their parents, but they had no rank. They could not earn, argue, or give anything back. Important men did not stop their work for them. The disciples are acting as most people would have expected: the teacher is busy with grown-up matters.

Luke says these were babies. His word is the one he used for the baby John leaping in Elizabeth's womb (1:41) and for the baby Jesus lying in the manger (2:12, 16). A baby cannot even come by itself. It has to be carried.

Luke places this scene straight after the Pharisee and the tax collector. The man who listed his good deeds went home without being made right. Now Jesus says the kingdom belongs to those who bring nothing at all.

The point of ‘like a little child’ is not that children are sweet or innocent. A child receives. A child cannot pay for a gift or earn a place. That is how the kingdom comes to anyone.
passages.ot: Israel's leaders laid their hands on children to bless them, as Jacob did with Joseph's sons (Genesis 48:14). And the psalmist pictures trust in God as a child at rest: “like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me” (Psalm 131:2).
passages.hard: Does this passage teach anything about baptizing babies? Some churches baptize infants, and many of them point to this passage, which shows that Jesus welcomed babies and blessed them. Other churches baptize only those old enough to confess faith, and they point out that Jesus blessed these children but did not baptize them. Christians hold both views with care, and these notes do not settle the question. All agree that no child is too small to matter to Jesus, and that no one should ever be kept from him.
passages.asks: The disciples thought babies were in the way. Ask who you have treated as an interruption: a child, someone who cannot give anything back. And ask whether you come to God as a child does, with empty hands, or with a list.

passages.t: The rich ruler, and the eye of a needle
passages.happening:
A ruler asks Jesus, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” (verse 18).

“Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replies. “No one is good except God alone” (verse 19). He reminds him of the commandments: do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honour your father and mother. “All these I have kept from my youth,” the man says (verse 21).

Jesus tells him, “You still lack one thing: Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me” (verse 22). The man becomes very sad, because he is extremely wealthy.

Jesus says, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God! Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (verses 24-25). The listeners ask, “Who then can be saved?” Jesus answers, “What is impossible with man is possible with God” (verse 27).

“Look,” says Peter, “we have left all we had to follow You” (verse 28). Jesus answers that no one who has left home or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God will fail to receive many times more now, and eternal life in the age to come.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 10:17-31; Matthew 19:16-30). Matthew calls the man young. Luke calls him a ruler, a man of standing, perhaps a leader in a synagogue or on a town council. In Luke, Jesus speaks after ‘seeing the man's sadness’ (verse 24). He is not glad to see him go.

His question has a strange shape. You do not ‘do’ something to inherit. An inheritance is given by someone else. Jesus' answer will show that eternal life is received, not earned.

Luke places this story right after the children. Jesus has just said the kingdom belongs to those who receive it like babies, with nothing in their hands. Now a man comes with full hands, and he cannot let go.

The camel was the largest animal in the land. The eye of a needle was the smallest opening anyone knew. Jesus is describing something impossible. Jewish teachers used the same kind of picture. The Babylonian Talmud, written down several centuries later, speaks of an elephant going through the eye of a needle as something that cannot happen (Berakhot 55b).

You may hear that the ‘Eye of the Needle’ was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall that a camel could squeeze through on its knees. There is no ancient evidence for such a gate. The story appears only many centuries later, and it softens what Jesus said.

Luke's list of what disciples leave includes ‘wife’, as his saying about hating father and mother did (14:26). Mark's list does not have it (Mark 10:29).
passages.ot:
The commandments Jesus names are from the second half of the Ten Commandments, the ones about how we treat other people (Exodus 20:12-16). He does not list the first ones, about loving God alone, or the last, ‘You shall not covet’ (Exodus 20:17). Many readers notice that the man's trouble lies exactly there: something else has first place in his heart.

And the Law itself taught that wealth must never become a rival god: “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3).
passages.hard:
‘Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone.’ Is Jesus saying he is not good, or not God? Readers take this in two main ways. Some think Jesus is pressing the man to think about what he has just said: if only God is good, and you call me good, what are you saying about me? Others think Jesus simply turns the man away from flattering a teacher and back to God. Either way, Jesus goes on to do what only God may do. He asks the man to give up everything to follow him.

Does Jesus ask every Christian to sell everything? The church has read this in two ways. Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian teacher in Egypt, wrote a whole sermon on this story, titled Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? He argued that Jesus asks us to be free from the love of money, not always to give it all away. Others have taken the words literally. A young Egyptian named Antony heard Matthew's version of this story read in church, gave away his family's land, and later went to live in the desert, as Athanasius tells in his Life of Antony. Many Christians since have followed one path or the other. In the next chapter Luke tells of Zacchaeus, a rich man who gives half his goods to the poor, and Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house” (19:9).

Is it wrong to be rich? Jesus does not say that wealth is evil. He says it makes entering the kingdom hard, so hard that only God can do it. Wealth tempts a person to trust what they own instead of God. But the answer in verse 27 is for everyone, rich or poor: no one gets in by their own strength. The poor are not saved by being poor either. Salvation is God's work for anyone. And this is no ground for contempt of the rich. Luke's own book shows wealthy people welcomed and changed.

The promise of ‘many times more’ (verse 30) has been used to promise money to those who give to a preacher. Luke's words do not allow that reading. What disciples receive is a new family of believers, who share their homes and lives, and eternal life in the age to come.
passages.asks: Jesus looked at the man's sadness and did not lower the price. Ask what your ‘one thing’ might be: the thing you could not let go of if he asked. Then remember verse 27. What is impossible for you is possible with God.

passages.t: The third warning: ‘we are going up to Jerusalem’
passages.happening:
Jesus takes the Twelve aside and says, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled” (verse 31). He will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted and spat on. “They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again” (verse 33).

“But the disciples did not understand any of these things. The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
This is the third time in Luke that Jesus tells his followers plainly what will happen to him (9:22; 9:44). Mark and Matthew give this warning too (Mark 10:32-34; Matthew 20:17-19).

People always spoke of going ‘up’ to Jerusalem. The city stands high in the hills, and the road climbs steeply from the Jordan valley.

The ‘Gentiles’ means non-Jews. Here it points to the Romans, who ruled Judea. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment.

Luke adds two things the others do not. First, Jesus says all this will happen as ‘the prophets have written’. His death will not be an accident or a defeat, but the fulfilment of Scripture. After he rises he will say the same thing again (24:25-27, 44-46). Second, Luke says three times over that the disciples did not understand: they did not understand, the meaning was hidden, they did not comprehend. They have just heard about giving up everything. They still cannot imagine their Master losing everything.
passages.ot: The prophets had written of a servant of God who would suffer: “I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle” (Isaiah 50:6). And a psalm of David cries, “All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads” (Psalm 22:7).
passages.hard: Why was the meaning ‘hidden’ from them? Luke does not say who hid it. Some readers think God kept them from understanding until after the resurrection, when Jesus “opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (24:45). Others think their own hopes for a conquering king made the words impossible to take in. Both may be true. Either way, Luke is honest that Jesus' closest friends did not understand the cross until afterwards. Readers who struggle with it are in good company.
passages.asks: The disciples heard the words and could not take them in. Ask what in Jesus' road to the cross you still find hard to accept: that God's way goes through suffering, or that he went that way for you. Ask him to open your mind, as he later opened theirs.

passages.happening:
As Jesus draws near to Jericho, a blind man is sitting by the road, begging. Hearing the crowd go by, he asks what is happening. They tell him, “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by” (verse 37).

So he calls out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (verse 38). Those at the front tell him to be quiet, but he cries out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” (verse 39).

Jesus stops and has the man brought to him. “What do you want Me to do for you?” he asks. “Lord,” he says, “let me see again.” “Receive your sight!” Jesus replies. “Your faith has healed you” (verse 42).

At once he can see, and he follows Jesus, glorifying God. And all the people who see it give praise to God.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 10:46-52; Matthew 20:29-34). Mark gives the man's name, Bartimaeus. Luke does not.

Jericho was the last town on the road up to Jerusalem from the Jordan valley, and at feast times the road was busy with pilgrims going up to the city. A blind man could not work, so he sat where the most people would pass and asked for help.

He calls Jesus ‘Son of David’. That was a title for the promised king, the descendant of David whom God had said would reign for ever. A blind beggar is the one who sees who Jesus is, and he says it out loud while others tell him to be quiet.

Jesus asks, ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ It is not a foolish question. Jesus treats the man as a person who can speak for himself, not just a problem to be fixed. And the man asks for something only God could give.

‘Let me see again’ suggests that he once could see. ‘Your faith has healed you’ can also be translated ‘your faith has saved you’, the same words Jesus spoke to the Samaritan leper (17:19). Then he follows Jesus up the road to Jerusalem. The disciples could not see what Jesus meant (verse 34). A blind man sees, and follows.
passages.ot: The prophets promised that when God came to save, “the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). In his first sermon Jesus read Isaiah's words about “recovery of sight to the blind” (Luke 4:18). And God had promised David, “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). The blind man is calling on that promise.
passages.hard:
Mark and Matthew say this happened as Jesus was leaving Jericho, and Matthew tells of two blind men. Luke tells of one man, as Jesus was coming near. How do these fit?

Readers have answered in several ways. Some suggest the man began calling out as Jesus came near and was healed as he left. Some note that there were two Jerichos in Jesus' day, the old ruined city and the newer town Herod had built near it, so that a person could be leaving one while coming near the other. Many scholars think Luke placed the healing before Jesus entered the city so that the story of Zacchaeus, inside Jericho, could follow it. Others hold that ancient writers, like good storytellers, shortened and arranged details without being thought false. On Matthew's two men, see the note on Matthew 20:29-34.

Christians who hold a high view of Scripture are found on more than one side here. These notes do not choose. What all three Gospels agree on is the heart of it: on the road near Jericho, a blind man cried to the Son of David for mercy, received his sight, and followed him.
passages.asks: The crowd told him to be quiet, and he shouted louder. Ask what you would say if Jesus stopped and asked you, ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ Say it honestly. Then, like the man who could see again, follow him.
